nameStory: Large Water-starwort gets its charming name from the star-like arrangement of its floating leaves at the water's surface. When viewed from above, these leaf clusters create perfect little green stars scattered across ponds and slow streams. The 'large' part distinguishes it from its smaller cousins in the water-starwort family.
description: Large Water-starwort is a delicate aquatic plant that spends most of its life completely underwater, with only its stem tips and leaf clusters floating at the surface. This unassuming plant forms small star-shaped rosettes of leaves that bob gently on still or slow-moving water. It's a small plant overall, rarely noticed unless you're looking closely at the water's surface. The tiny flowers are so small they're barely visible to the naked eye.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Almost entirely submerged with only the very tips of stems floating at the surface, creating small star-shaped leaf clusters that drift on the water

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Floating leaves are arranged in star-like rosettes of 6-8 leaves, feeling soft and slightly rubbery when gently touched; submerged leaves are narrow and ribbon-like

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Extremely tiny flowers, barely visible without magnification, appearing as minute bumps among the floating leaf clusters throughout the growing season

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Found in still or very slow-moving water like pond edges, quiet stream backwaters, and shallow wetland areas where it can anchor to muddy bottoms

habitat: Look for Large Water-starwort in quiet waters throughout New England - shallow ponds, slow-moving streams, marshy areas, and mudflats. It prefers spots with soft, muddy bottoms where its roots can anchor, typically in water less than a few feet deep. You'll often find it mixed with other aquatic plants in protected coves and backwater areas.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as water warms, with fresh green star-shaped leaf clusters appearing at the surface as stems stretch upward from overwintered roots.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with the most visible floating leaf rosettes and continuous tiny flower production throughout the warm months.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to die back as water cools, though some leaf clusters may persist into early fall in protected areas.
seasonality.winter: Above-water portions die back completely, but roots survive in the mud to regrow the following spring.

funFact: Despite producing flowers throughout the entire growing season, Large Water-starwort's blooms are so incredibly tiny that most people walk right past this plant their entire lives without ever noticing it's flowering - each bloom is smaller than the head of a pin!
confusionNotes: The star-shaped floating leaf clusters are quite distinctive, but beginners might mistake young water lily seedlings for water-starwort. Remember that water lily leaves are round or heart-shaped, while water-starwort leaves are narrow and arranged in perfect star patterns.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting it's 'large,' this is actually a quite small plant - the name only means it's larger than other water-starwort species. Don't expect to find a big, showy aquatic plant when searching for this modestly-sized species.
compareHints: Large Water-starwort differs from its relatives like Narrow-fruited Water-starwort mainly in the size and arrangement of its floating leaves - it has broader leaves in more prominent star-shaped clusters. Pond Water-starwort tends to stay more completely submerged, while Terrestrial Water-starwort can actually grow on muddy shores out of water entirely.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's water-starworts, Narrow-fruited Water-starwort has the slenderest seed pods, while Pond Water-starwort has rounder, broader fruits.
Pond water-starwort differs from its relatives like narrow-fruited water-starwort by preferring completely still water rather than flowing streams.

Unlike its aquatic relatives like Pond Water-starwort and Large Water-starwort, Terrestrial Water-starwort has adapted to completely dry conditions and forms ground-hugging mats rather than floating rosettes.
